reference.source: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice / Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies
clinicalPearls: Characteristic immunophenotype is low or absent IgG, IgA and IgE with normal or raised IgM, reflecting failure of immunoglobulin class-switch recombination
The X-linked form (CD40 ligand deficiency, CD40LG) is the most common and typically presents in infant boys with recurrent sinopulmonary infection

CD40 ligand deficiency behaves as a combined immunodeficiency, with susceptibility to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, Cryptosporidium, and other opportunistic organisms in addition to encapsulated bacteria
Autosomal recessive forms from AID (AICDA) or UNG defects are purely B-cell (humoral) and lack the opportunistic infection risk seen with the CD40 pathway defects
Neutropenia, oral ulceration and sclerosing cholangitis (often Cryptosporidium-associated) are recognised complications of the CD40L/CD40 subtypes
Lymphoid hyperplasia with enlarged tonsils and lymph nodes is typical of the AID-deficient form
Immunoglobulin replacement is the mainstay of humoral support, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative for the CD40L/CD40 combined phenotypes
reference.pathophysiology: Hyper-IgM syndromes arise from defects in the molecular machinery that allows activated B cells to switch from producing IgM to producing IgG, IgA and IgE and to undergo affinity maturation. In the X-linked form, mutations in the gene encoding CD40 ligand on activated T cells prevent effective engagement of CD40 on B cells and other antigen-presenting cells, disrupting both antibody class-switching and cell-mediated immune signalling. Autosomal recessive variants involve CD40 itself or the downstream B-cell enzymes activation-induced cytidine deaminase and uracil-N-glycosylase, which are required for class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation. The result is a failure to generate mature isotype antibody responses, leaving normal or elevated IgM but deficient protective immunoglobulin.
additionalDifferentials: Severe combined immunodeficiency (for the CD40L/CD40 combined phenotype)
Specific antibody deficiency with normal immunoglobulins
Secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia from protein loss or immunosuppression
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative serum immunoglobulins showing low IgG/IgA/IgE with normal or high IgM
Flow cytometry for CD40 ligand expression on activated CD4 T cells
Lymphocyte subset enumeration and specific antibody responses to protein and polysaccharide antigens
Molecular genetic testing of CD40LG, CD40, AICDA and UNG
Screening for Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium and liver involvement in the CD40 pathway subtypes
Full blood count to detect associated neutropenia
redFlags: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia or other opportunistic infection in an infant boy
Cryptosporidial infection with sclerosing cholangitis or progressive liver disease
Persistent or cyclical neutropenia with oral ulceration and sepsis risk
Failure to thrive with recurrent invasive infection
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on subtype: the autosomal recessive humoral forms generally do well on immunoglobulin replacement, whereas untreated CD40 ligand or CD40 deficiency carries high morbidity from opportunistic infection, liver disease and malignancy, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the prospect of cure when performed early.
pitfalls: Labelling the condition as a pure antibody deficiency and missing the combined immunodeficiency behaviour of the CD40L/CD40 subtypes
Failing to institute Pneumocystis prophylaxis in the CD40 pathway forms
Overlooking Cryptosporidium as a cause of chronic diarrhoea and biliary disease
Attributing raised IgM to infection alone and not pursuing class-switch defect testing
